title: Ecosystem Dynamics: Interactions, Energy and Populations
seo_title: Year 11 Biology: Ecosystem Dynamics Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Interactions between organisms (predation, competition, symbiosis); keystone species and niches; energy flow, trophic levels and productivity; population growth and carrying capacity; succession and the effects of disturbance and introduced species. (Senior Secondary Biology, Unit 1: Biodiversity and the interconnectedness of life)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Biology worksheets on ecosystem dynamics: symbiosis, keystone species, energy flow, productivity, the 10% rule, population growth, carrying capacity and succession. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Energy flows through ecosystems; matter cycles.
key_sub: About 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.
body_html:
How to think about it

Organisms interact by predation, competition and symbiosis (mutualism, commensalism, parasitism). A keystone species, such as an apex predator, has a large effect on its community.

Producers fix energy; at each trophic level most energy is used in respiration and lost as heat, so only about 10% passes on. Net primary productivity = gross primary productivity − respiration.

Populations grow until limiting factors hold them near the carrying capacity. After disturbance, communities change by succession.

Example

Producers fix 20 000 kJ. How much reaches the secondary consumers (10% rule)?

20 000 × 0.1 = 2000 kJ (primary)

2000 × 0.1

Answer: 200 kJ

Example

GPP = 5000, respiration = 3000 (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹). NPP?

NPP = GPP − R

Answer: 2000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹

Common mistakes

  • Saying energy is recycled: only matter is recycled.
  • Mixing up commensalism (one unaffected) and mutualism (both benefit).
  • Thinking a population keeps growing forever: limiting factors set a carrying capacity.

faq.q: What is the difference between gross and net primary productivity?
faq.a: GPP is all the energy fixed by producers; NPP is what is left after their respiration, available to consumers.

faq.q: What makes a species a keystone species?
faq.a: Its effect on the ecosystem is far larger than its numbers suggest; removing it changes the whole community, as with apex predators or reef-building corals.

items.q: What is secondary succession?
c: regrowth of a community where soil remains after a disturbance such as fire
a food chain with two consumers
items.e: It is faster because soil and seeds are already there.

items.q: Reef-building corals and the algae (zooxanthellae) in their tissues both benefit. What is this relationship?
items.e: The algae give sugars; the coral gives shelter and nutrients.

items.q: Two species of honeyeater feed on the same flowers. What is this?
items.e: Competition between different species.

items.q: Cane toads were introduced to Queensland in 1935. Why have they harmed native predators?
c: toads eat all the eucalyptus leaves
the toads are toxic and predators such as quolls die after eating them
items.e: Northern quoll numbers dropped as toads spread.

items.q: Rabbits were released in Australia in 1859 and spread rapidly. Why did their population grow so fast?
c: the climate was too cold for them
they had plenty of food and few predators or diseases
items.e: Myxoma virus and calicivirus were later released to control them.

items.q: Dingoes control kangaroo and fox numbers in some areas. What role does this suggest dingoes play?
items.e: Apex predators shape the whole food web.

items.q: A forest fire burns trees but leaves the soil. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Which factor is density-independent?
c: disease spreading through a crowded colony
predation that increases with prey numbers
items.e: Drought affects a population whatever its density.

items.q: Lava cools into new bare rock. Lichens grow first. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: A landslide scrapes a slope down to bare bedrock. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Why do many Australian plants, such as banksias, depend on fire?
c: their leaves need ash to photosynthesise
heat or smoke triggers their seeds to be released or to germinate
fire adds nitrogen gas to the air
items.e: Many species are adapted to particular fire regimes.

items.q: A new volcanic island rises from the sea. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: A population of 640 deer has 17 births, 3 immigrants, 6 deaths and 24 emigrants in a year. What is the population at the end of the year?
items.e: Nt+1 = Nt + (B + I) − (D + E) = 630.

items.q: A farm field is abandoned and weeds move in. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Clownfish shelter in sea anemones and keep them clean; the anemone's stinging cells protect the fish. What is this relationship?
items.e: Both species benefit.

items.q: A population of 560 deer has 39 births, 9 immigrants, 16 deaths and 22 emigrants in a year. What is the population at the end of the year?
items.e: Nt+1 = Nt + (B + I) − (D + E) = 570.

items.q: A population of 240 deer has 57 births, 17 immigrants, 33 deaths and 10 emigrants in a year. What is the population at the end of the year?
items.e: Nt+1 = Nt + (B + I) − (D + E) = 271.

items.q: What does the competitive exclusion principle state?
c: two species cannot share exactly the same niche for long in one place
items.e: One species will outcompete the other.

items.q: A population of 400 deer has 19 births, 13 immigrants, 59 deaths and 5 emigrants in a year. What is the population at the end of the year?
items.e: Nt+1 = Nt + (B + I) − (D + E) = 368.

items.q: Which interaction is shown when a lyrebird and a bandicoot both dig in the leaf litter for the same insects?
items.e: Two species use the same limited resource.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 40000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 40000 × 0.13 = 40.0 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 50 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 50 × 10³ = 50000 J.

items.q: Which process returns nutrients from dead organisms to the soil?
items.e: Decomposers recycle matter, not energy.

items.q: Why is energy lost between trophic levels?
c: much is used in respiration and released as heat, and some is in undigested waste
all the energy is stored as biomass
energy is destroyed at each level
items.e: Typically only about 10% passes to the next level.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 60 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 60 × 10³ = 60000 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 30 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 30 × 10³ = 30000 J.

items.q: What is the role of producers?
c: releasing all their energy as heat
converting light energy into chemical energy in organic molecules
items.e: Producers fix energy by photosynthesis.

items.q: A single eucalyptus supports thousands of caterpillars. What shape is the pyramid of numbers?
c: inverted at the base (one producer, many consumers)
items.e: Pyramids of numbers can be inverted; pyramids of energy cannot.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 1000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 1000 × 0.12 = 10.0 J.

items.q: In a food web, what happens to the number of crickets if most of the frogs that eat them are removed?
items.e: Less predation lets the prey population grow.

items.q: What does a pyramid of biomass show?
c: the dry mass of organisms at each trophic level
the number of organisms at each level
items.e: Biomass is measured per unit area.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 10 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 10 × 10³ = 10000 J.

items.q: The primary consumers contain 15000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the secondary consumers contain 1200 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 8.00%.

items.q: What is a trophic level?
c: a feeding position in a food chain
the number of organisms in a habitat
items.e: Producers are level 1, herbivores level 2.

items.q: Which statement about matter and energy in ecosystems is correct?
c: energy is recycled, but matter is lost
matter is recycled, but energy flows through and is lost as heat
items.e: Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 1000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 1000 × 0.13 = 1.00 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 7000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 7000 × 0.12 = 70.0 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 100000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 100000 × 0.13 = 100 J.

items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 400000 × 0.13 = 400 J.

items.q: What is the first link of a detritus food chain?
items.e: Decomposers break it down.

items.q: A crop has a gross primary production of 18000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and loses 8100 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ in respiration. Calculate its net primary production.
items.e: NPP = GPP − R = 9900 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: The producers contain 20000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the primary consumers contain 3000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 15.0%.

items.q: A crop has a gross primary production of 12000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and loses 7800 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ in respiration. Calculate its net primary production.
items.e: NPP = GPP − R = 4200 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: What is net production in a consumer?
c: chemical energy in food minus energy lost in faeces, urine and respiration
items.e: N = I − (F + R).

items.q: A crop has a gross primary production of 36000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and loses 19800 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ in respiration. Calculate its net primary production.
items.e: NPP = GPP − R = 16200 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: A bushland has a net primary production of 12600 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and respiratory losses of 23400 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the gross primary production.
items.e: GPP = NPP + R = 36000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: The primary consumers contain 8000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the secondary consumers contain 400 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 5.00%.

items.q: What is the main reason energy is lost between trophic levels?
c: respiration releases heat, and some parts are not eaten or digested
items.e: Typically only about 10% is passed on.

items.q: A crop has a gross primary production of 25000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and loses 12500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ in respiration. Calculate its net primary production.
items.e: NPP = GPP − R = 12500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: What is leaching?
c: nitrates are washed out of soil into rivers and lakes
items.e: It can cause eutrophication.

items.q: A bushland has a net primary production of 16000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and respiratory losses of 24000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the gross primary production.
items.e: GPP = NPP + R = 40000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: What is denitrification?
c: bacteria convert nitrates into nitrogen gas in waterlogged soil
items.e: It happens in anaerobic conditions.

items.q: The producers contain 10000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the primary consumers contain 800 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 8.00%.

items.q: A bushland has a net primary production of 9900 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and respiratory losses of 8100 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the gross primary production.
items.e: GPP = NPP + R = 18000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: What is ecological succession?
c: a gradual, predictable change in the species of an area leading to a climax community
items.e: Pioneer species come first.

items.q: Why are food chains usually limited to 3–4 trophic levels?
c: too little energy is left at higher levels
items.e: Most energy is lost as heat.

items.q: A crop has a gross primary production of 20000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and loses 9000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ in respiration. Calculate its net primary production.
items.e: NPP = GPP − R = 11000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: A crop has a gross primary production of 15000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and loses 7500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ in respiration. Calculate its net primary production.
items.e: NPP = GPP − R = 7500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: A bushland has a net primary production of 13500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and respiratory losses of 16500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the gross primary production.
items.e: GPP = NPP + R = 30000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

items.q: A remora fish attaches to a shark and eats scraps of its food; the shark is not affected. What is this relationship?
items.e: One benefits, the other is unaffected.

the place where a species lives only
